10429-miss-lulu-bett:
Zona Gale published this novel in 1921, following its heroine month by month from April through September. Lulu Bett lives with the Deacon family, serving at table under a gas jet, while Mr. Deacon jokes nightly and Mrs. Deacon speaks gently to all. The small tulip plant on the table hints at Lulu's own stifled life.

As months pass, Lulu faces family duty, a child's needs, and a chance for a life of her own. Gale writes with humor, pity, and close detail about women's work in a small town. Readers get a keen, humane novel of a woman finding voice, later famous on stage and in film.
10440-tutt-and-mr-tutt:
Arthur Train published this law story collection in 1919, following the firm of Tutt and Tutt, attorneys in New York. The elder Mr. Tutt and his junior partner Tutt take cases where chance, not grand design, often decides the outcome. Train, himself a lawyer, writes with wit and inside knowledge.

The human element, mock hen and mock turtle, Samuel and Delilah, the dog Andrew, and Lallapaloosa Limited fill the set. A murder client who boasts he would kill again opens the first tale. Readers get a clever, humane book of legal comedy and courtroom craft.
20932-advice-to-a-young-man-upon-first-g:
Joy at a young man's entry to Oxford opens Advice to a Young Man in ten letters. The writer's own Oxford days warm his hopes for the youth's gain. Edward Berens frames his counsel as trust in the place's deep benefits.

Study, friends, money, faith, and time all get plain, fatherly treatment here. Such letter guides steered new undergraduates through a famed, risky world. Berens warns and cheers in equal measure across the ten letters. The book preserves the morals and manners expected at Oxford in the early 1800s, in a voice both kind and firmly of its age.
21634-the-life-and-adventures-of-nat-lov:
Nat Love tells his own life in The Life and Adventures of Nat Love, published at Los Angeles in 1907. In the cattle country he was better known as Deadwood Dick. The book is dedicated to his wife, Alice Love, and illustrated with family pictures.

Love begins with slavery days on the old plantation, and a stolen jug that gave him his first drunk. Freedom, his father's death, and work at a dollar and a half a month follow. Then come Texas cowboys, brand reading, round-ups, and fights on the trail. Few Black cowboys left so full a record of the range.
290-the-stark-munro-letters-being-series:
J. Stark Munro, a young doctor, writes twelve letters to his friend Herbert Swanborough between 1881 and 1884. The Stark Munro Letters, edited and arranged by Arthur Conan Doyle, follow a beginner facing money trouble and religious doubt. Doyle's preface hands the letters on as a plain account.

Two letters, the fifth and ninth, carry excisions, but the rest stand as written. Munro's struggles with practice, faith, and friendship give the book its shape. Doyle promises strength to any young man in the same valley. The novel reads as a frank portrait of starting out.
8680-the-story-of-kennett:
Bayard Taylor sets this novel in Kennett, the Pennsylvania countryside he knew well, and dedicates it to his friends and neighbours there. In his prologue he tells them plainly that many will live in the very houses and till the very fields he gives his characters. Will judge whether he drew them with the simple truth he aimed at. He asks their pardon for any failure, and thanks them for quiet, happy years among them.

The story that follows grows out of that soil: farm families, local customs, love, and rivalry in a Quaker-influenced community. Taylor writes with a neighbour's eye for work, worship, and talk, rather than a tourist's romance. Readers of American regional fiction will find a warm, grounded novel. A portrait of Chester County life that its first readers could check against their own front doors.
9597-the-inner-life-part-3-from-the-work:
Part three of Whittier's Inner Life gathers essays on evil, faith, and the Quaker way. The Agency of Evil opens, asking where sin and suffering come from in a world full of mystery. Hamlet Among the Graves, Swedenborg, and The Better Land follow, with Dora Greenwell and The Society of Friends. John Woolman's Journal and Haverford College close the run.

Whittier weighs dark riddles with a Quaker's trust in inward light, not with cold systems. His prose stays plain and earnest, aimed at the heart. A reader gets a thoughtful set of spiritual essays, where a poet faces evil, death, and hope with quiet faith.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-eichstatt:
Eichstatt is a diocese in Bavaria, north of the Danube and suffragan to Bamberg, whose story the entry traces from its founding to 1909. Saint Boniface set it up, making his nephew Saint Willibald abbot and regional bishop in 741 and fixing the diocese in 745. Willibald brought his brother Wunibald and sister Walburga to help, built Heidenheim monastery for them, and ran a flourishing school at Eichstatt until his death in 781.

His successors number seventy-five in an unbroken line. Bishop Erchanbold laid the ground for the see's worldly power. It grew through the Hirschberg inheritance of 1305. By then the bishops ruled a land of some four hundred and thirty-seven square miles and fifty-six thousand people. Secularisation in 1803 handed those lands to Bavaria. Among the bishops, Reginold shone as poet and musician, and Gundekar II rebuilt the cathedral and wrote its bishops' lives.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-francis-xavie:
Francis Xavier Witt, born at Walderbach in the Upper Palatinate on 9 February 1834 and dead at Landshut on 2 December 1888. He was a priest, composer, and reformer of church music who founded the St. Cecilia Society for German-speaking lands. Ordained on 11 June 1856, he served as assistant pastor while studying music in all its branches.

In 1859 he became teacher of Gregorian chant, homiletics, and catechetics at the Ratisbon seminary, then director of the Sodality of the Blessed Virgin and choirmaster at St. Emmeran. His compositions, more than twenty masses for voices with organ, orchestra, or unaccompanied, plus litanies, motets, and music for the whole liturgical year, remain standard repertoire in the best choirs. They are praised for fine construction, spontaneity, and organic cohesion.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-gaspar-schott:
Gaspar Schott, a German Jesuit physicist born at Königshofen in 1608, woke scientific curiosity across Germany. He entered the Society in 1627, finished his studies in Sicily amid political turmoil, taught at Palermo, and studied under Kircher at Rome. After some thirty years abroad he returned home and spent his last years teaching and writing at Augsburg, dying in 1666.

Schott's books overflow with curious facts and trials, once widely read. His Universal Magic of Nature and Art, four volumes from 1657 to 1659, gathers mathematical puzzles and trials in optics and sound. His Hydraulic-Pneumatic Mechanics gave the first printed account of Guericke's air pump. A Curious Physics, a study of springs and rivers, and a mathematics course followed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-james-robert-:
Parliamentary barrister James Robert Hope-Scott, originally Hope, was born at Great Marlow, Berkshire, on 15 July 1812. He died in London on 29 April 1873. He was third son of Sir Alexander Hope, fourth son of John, second Earl of Hopetoun. His mother was the third and youngest daughter of George Brown of Ellerton. During childhood his home was Sandhurst Military College, where his father commanded. Afterwards he traveled with his parents through Dresden, Lausanne, and Florence.

Thus he mastered German, French, and Italian. In 1825 he entered Eton, and in 1828 he matriculated at Christ Church, Oxford. After a Paris visit in 1829 he took up Oxford residence that year. He took his B.A. in 1832, placing fourth class in literis humanioribus. Next year he became a fellow of Merton College. The entry opens the life of a Tractarian lawyer whose scholarship and conversions shaped Victorian Catholicism.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-john-hewett:
John Hewett, also recorded as Weldon, was an English martyr executed in the Armada year of 1588. Son of William Hewett of York, he passed from Caius College, Cambridge, to the English College at Reims, where he received minor orders in 1583. Captured in England and banished, he reached Reims again in 1585, was ordained, and returned, only to be captured and exiled to the Netherlands.

There the Earl of Leicester had him arrested on a false accusation and sent back for trial. In October 1588 he was arraigned for taking ordination from Rome and entering England to work as a priest. Sentenced to death, he was taken through London streets to Mile End Green, where before execution he disputed with two preachers. That the two names denote one martyr is proved by a tract of 24 October 1588 reporting the trial and speeches of Weldon, Hartley, and Sutton.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-joshua-basset:
Joshua Bassett was an English scholar who became Master of Sidney Sussex College under James II. Born about 1641 at Lynn Regis, he entered Gonville and Caius College in 1657, took degrees through 1671, and rose to senior fellow. By the king's mandate he was elected Master of Sidney Sussex in December 1686 without the usual oaths.

In January 1687 Bassett declared himself a Catholic, had Mass said in his rooms, and changed statutes that barred his co-religionists. He clashed with the university over a degree for the Benedictine Alban Francis and banned a Guy Fawkes Day service. After the Revolution he fled the college and died in extreme poverty at London in 1720.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-marquard-herr:
Marquard Herrgott was a Benedictine historian and diplomat, born at Freiburg in 1694 and dead at Krozingen in 1762. After humanities at Freiburg and Strasburg, he tutored a private family and followed two pupils to Paris for two years. On return he joined St Blasien Abbey in the Black Forest, vowing in 1715 and studying theology at Rome.

Ordained in 1718, he returned to St Blasien, studied Oriental tongues at St Gall in 1721, and soon went to Vienna with his abbot to study history. He then worked under Maurist Benedictines at Saint-Germain-des-Pres, producing Vetus disciplina monastica at Paris in 1726 on old monastic customs. In 1728 Vienna made him diplomatic envoy of the Breisgau Estates, a post he held creditably over twenty years. There he studied Habsburg history for eight years and published his Genealogia diplomatica in 1737, followed by Monumenta volumes in 1750, 1753, and 1760.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-missal-of-arb:
The Missal of Arbuthnott is a handwritten Scottish Mass book, penned in 1491 by James Sibbald, priest of Arbuthnott in Scotland, for his own church. After the Reformation it came, along with two further manuscripts in the same hand, into the Arbuthnott family's keeping, where it stayed until 1897.

In that year Archibald Coats of Paisley bought it and presented it to the Paisley museum. The manuscript, written on vellum in large Gothic characters with numerous miniatures, illuminated capitals, and borders, consists of 244 leaves and is complete. It also contains a full-length painting of St. Ternan, the patron of Arbuthnott, making it a treasure of late medieval Scottish devotion.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-peter-hardema:
Peter Hardeman Burnett was the first American governor of California, born at Nashville in 1807. Raised in Missouri's rough conditions, he married Harriet Rogers, studied law, was admitted to the bar in 1839, and edited a Missouri weekly. Moving to Oregon in 1843, he helped frame its territorial government and sat in its legislature. A published debate between Alexander Campbell and Bishop Purcell shook his Protestant faith.

Systematic study led him to Rome, and he was received into the Catholic Church at Oregon City in June 1846. In California from 1848 he sat in the assembly, became a superior court judge in 1849, helped frame the state constitution, and served as chief justice. That November he was chosen governor, the first to hold the office under American statehood. He died at San Francisco in 1895.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-sebastian-wes:
Sebastian Westcott, English organist born about 1524, sang as a boy chorister at St Paul's Cathedral in London under Redford. In 1550 he took three posts there at once: organist, almoner, and master of the boys. He held his post under Edward VI, Mary, and Elizabeth from 1550 to 1583, despite standing openly for the ancient faith, for which he suffered deprivation and prison. His entry in the 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia celebrates Master Sebastian.

His fame rests chiefly on plays and pageants with music, staged for the English court over thirty-three years by the cathedral schoolboys. So celebrated was he that writers seldom use his surname, calling him almost always Master Sebastian. Under Mary he arranged music for the formal restoration of the old faith at St Paul's in November 1553. He also composed a Te Deum sung on 9 February 1554 after Wyatt's rebellion failed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-thomas-edward:
Thomas Edward Bridgett, priest and author, was born at Derby in 1829 to Protestant parents and died at Clapham in 1899. His father, a silk manufacturer, sent him to Mill Hill, Tonbridge and St. John's College, Cambridge. Unable to swear the oath of royal supremacy, he left Cambridge in 1850, heard Newman lecture, and was received into the Catholic Church that June.

He joined the Redemptorists in Belgium and was ordained in 1856. He served at Clapham and Limerick, where in 1868 he founded the Confraternity of the Holy Family for men, soon over five thousand strong. As a writer he is best known for lives of John Fisher and other English Catholic figures, blending scholarship with missionary zeal.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ven-james-duc:
James Duckett was a martyr born at Gilfortrigs in Skelsmergh parish, Westmoreland, at an uncertain date, of an ancient county family, who died on 9 April 1601. He worked as a bookseller and publisher in London. His godfather was the martyr James Leybourn of Skelsmergh. Brought up Protestant, he was converted while an apprentice in London by a Catholic book a friend lent him.

Before he could enter the church he was twice jailed for skipping Protestant service, and he had to buy out his apprenticeship and leave his master. At last a venerable priest named Weekes, jailed in the Gatehouse at Westminster, reconciled him. After two or three years he married a Catholic widow. Of twelve years of married life no fewer than nine were spent in prison, for spreading Catholic books and holding fast to his new-found faith, before his arrest and execution.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ven-john-duck:
John Duckett was a martyr, probably a grandson of James Duckett, born at Underwinder in Sedbergh parish, Yorkshire, in 1603, who died on 7 September 1644. Ordained priest in 1639, he then went to Paris and studied three years at the College of Arras. He possessed an extraordinary gift of prayer, and even as a student he would spend whole nights in contemplation.

En route to the English mission, he passed two months in spiritual exercises guided by his uncle, Nieuport's Carthusian prior. He laboured about a year in Durham and was seized near Whittingham on his way to baptize two children on 2 July 1644. Tradition marks his arrest place with a tall stone cross. Carried to Sunderland, examined by a Parliamentary committee, and put in irons, he was condemned and suffered.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ven-montford-:
Montford Scott was an English martyr born in Norfolk, martyred at Fleet Street in London on 2 July 1591. He entered Douai College in 1574, among its earliest students, and studied theology. The next year he became subdeacon and accompanied Dominic Vaughan to England. In Essex they fell into government hands in December 1576, and under examination Vaughan weakly betrayed the names of Catholics in London and Essex.

Handed by the Privy Council to the Archbishop of Canterbury for further questioning, they gave up nothing more and were afterwards set free. Scott returned to Douai on 22 May 1577, was ordained priest at Brussels, and set out for the English mission on 17 June. His crossing vessel was attacked by pirates, but he escaped with his life. The entry follows his later mission years and his execution.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ven-ralph-cro:
Ralph Crockett was an English martyr born at Barton near Farndon in Cheshire, executed at Chichester on 1 October 1588. Schooled at Cambridge and ordained at Reims in 1585, he was captured aboard ship at Littlehampton in Sussex with three other priests. They were Thomas Bramston, George Potter, and his fellow martyr Edward James, born at Breaston in Derbyshire about 1557.

James was schooled at Derby Grammar School, then St John's College, Oxford, and the English colleges at Reims and Rome, before Bishop Goldwell of St Asaph ordained him in October 1583. All four were sent to London and jailed on 27 April 1586. After the Armada's failure the government resolved to avenge itself on priests in custody. Crockett and James, with John Oven and Francis Edwardes, were chosen for trial at Chichester on 30 September and executed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-venerable-tho:
Thomas Sprott, or Spratt, was a Westmorland priest executed at Lincoln in July 1600 with Thomas Hunt. Born at Skelsmergh near Kendal, Sprott was ordained from Douai in 1596, sent to England the same year. Signed a 1598 letter to the pope favouring an archpriest, a chief priest, for England.

Hunt, a Norfolk priest trained at Seville, had escaped from Wisbech prison months earlier. The two were arrested at the Saracen's Head in Lincoln when holy oils and two breviaries, priests' prayer books, were found in their baggage. At trial neither priesthood was proved nor confessed and no evidence was produced, yet Judge Sir John Glanville directed the jury to convict, which it did. Glanville died sixteen days later under unusual circumstances, as the entry records.
cicero-catilinarian-orations-upcott:
Cicero's Catilinarian Orations are four speeches he gave in 63 BC as consul of Rome, against the conspirator Catiline. E. A. Upcott's Oxford translation is the text here. Catiline, a ruined aristocrat, was plotting to seize the state with an army raised in Etruria.

The first speech, delivered in the Senate with Catiline present, opens with the famous cry: how long will you abuse our patience? Cicero lays out the plot, drives Catiline from the city, and reports the arrest of his partners in Rome. The speeches saved the republic and made Cicero's name as an orator. They have been school models of rhetoric ever since.
doe-osti-3012257-evaluating-movement-pat: Hanford elk got movement-evaluated, and this DOE text tracks the Rattlesnake Hills herd. The pages detail the 2019-2024 findings. The ecologists get their data. The herd was elk. The data were ecologist. The years were 2019-2024. The hills were Rattlesnake. The elk were Hanford.
doe-osti-3024733-new-correlated-numerica: Attoseconds are billionths of a billionth of a second — the timescale on which electrons move. Luca Argenti's work builds new computer methods that track one or two electrons being knocked out of a molecule that fast. The tools let physicists test ideas about nature's fastest processes.
doe-osti-3409467-theoretical-high-energy: HEP theory got lattice-methoded, and this DOE text covers theoretical high energy physics. The pages detail the theoretical findings. The physicists get their data. The methods were lattice. The data were physicist. The high were energy. The lattice were methods.
doe-osti-3683731-mach-14-thermometry-usi: Mach 14 got Rayleigh-thermometried, and this DOE text covers scattering thermometry. The pages detail the Mach findings. The engineers get their data. The scattering was Rayleigh. The data were engineer. The 14 were Mach. The thermometry were scattering. The Rayleigh were engineers.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-BremerGeorgeWal:
Arthur Bremer shot George Wallace in May 1972, crippling the Alabama governor during his presidential campaign. This Washington Post article by Philip A. McCombs reports what Bremer's diary revealed: before Wallace, his intended target had been President Richard Nixon.

The diary describes Bremer following Nixon back to Washington from Ottawa in April 1972, after missing six chances to shoot him there. Bremer wrote his way toward an assassination, and the diary became the record of that drift. The article preserves the news as it broke, when the Wallace shooting suddenly looked like the second act of a plan aimed at a president.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-JacksonEverett_:
Fenton Wheeler reported for the Associated Press under the headline Plane Blasted. Cuba had shot down and captured Everett Jackson, an American former paratrooper. Jackson's flight ended after he dropped a package containing a rifle over Cuba on December 29.

Arms drops to anti-Castro fighters were a running feature of the exile war. A lone plane, a rifle package, and a capture made a compact Cold War story, and the wire carried it in a few lines. The article preserves Jackson's fate as American readers learned it, in the flat tone of the wire.
mental-defectives-and-sexual-offenders-r:
New Zealand's Committee of Inquiry issued this report in 1925. The Minister of Health, Sir Maui Pomare, appointed the committee. Its chairman was W. H. Triggs, and its members included doctors, prison officials, and educators. The report was laid before the House of Representatives.

The committee examined how the young country dealt with mental deficiency and sexual offending. Part One traces the history of the problem and earlier policy. Members drew on medical, school, and prison experience across the dominion. The document records the official attitudes and terms of its era, which many modern readers will find harsh.
miss-lulu-bett:
Zona Gale published this novel in 1921 and built it month by month. Six chapters run from April to September. The opening scene sets the Deacon family at supper under a flaring gas jet. Mr. Deacon jokes about turning down the gas, as he does nearly every night, and calls the plain meal festive.

Lulu Bett, the wife's sister, lives in the Deacon household as its unpaid drudge. Gale watches the family's small tyrannies with a precise, quiet irony. The tulip plant on the table, lit by gaslight, sets the tone of stunted lives. Across one spring and summer, Lulu's patience and dignity come to a crisis.
nasa-tm-19670009381-greenhouse-effect-in:
R. E. Samuelson, of NASA's Goddard Space Flight Center in Maryland, models an idealized planet atmosphere in this paper. The atmosphere is semi-infinite, plane-parallel, and filled with scattering particles. An outside point source shines visible light on it, and the layer sits in radiative balance.

Samuelson extends the method of discrete ordinates to describe the setup. He computes the steady pattern of thermal radiation and the matching temperature structure with depth. The greenhouse factor, he finds, approaches a finite limit deep down. Multiple scattering proves extremely effective at heating the lower regions, a result he connects with Venus.
nasa-tm-19710012521-selection-of-landing:
Staff of the Landing and Recovery Division at the Manned Spacecraft Center in Houston issued this internal note, MSC-02666, on September 25, 1970. It selects landing airfields for space shuttle orbiters. Early shuttle designs varied in crossrange, meaning how far sideways the orbiter could steer during its glide home. Each crossrange value opened a different set of usable runways.

The note presents the chosen airfields in tables and maps. Planners could match an orbiter design against fields it could actually reach. Work like this shaped early shuttle planning. Safe landing options had to exist for normal returns and for emergencies across the flight path.
our-stage-and-its-critics-by-e-f-s-of-th: Edward Fordham Spence, dramatic critic of the Westminster Gazette, published Our Stage and Its Critics in 1910. It is a practitioner's anatomy of his own trade. The hosted sample shows the title page and a contents list only. Long chapter summaries appear with it. The chapters promise the critic's qualifications, duties, and stock phrases. His fear of libel and his duty to be tolerant follow. Plays of particular types close the plan. No page of Spence's argument appears.
sir-walter-scott:
Richard H. Hutton published this short life of Sir Walter Scott with Macmillan in London in 1878. A prefatory note owns that most of the book draws, in one form or other, on Lockhart's ten-volume life of Scott. No sound introduction to Scott could skip that source, Hutton holds.

Scott's own writings and Lockhart's life stand as the great authorities on his character and story, Hutton states. On the one dispute, Scott's dealings with the Ballantyne brothers, Hutton checked Lockhart against the brothers' own side. Gladstone's praise of Lockhart's life, voiced ten years before, opens the case for this compact life.
south-with-scott: Rear-Admiral Edward R. G. R. Evans wrote South with Scott, with maps and photos, printed by Collins' Clear-Type Press at London and Glasgow. Evans gives the book to Lashly and Crean. The opening pages name the shore party: Robert Falcon Scott, captain, as owner and boss; Evans himself as Teddy; Victor L. A. Campbell as the Wicked Mate; and Henry R. Bowers as Birdie, with Lawrence E. G. Oates as Titus the soldier.
the-act-of-incorporation-and-the-by-laws:
The Act of Incorporation and the By-Laws of the Massachusetts Homoeopathic Medical Society was printed at Boston by Fred Rogers of Washington Street in 1864. It sets out the society's legal birth and its rules in full.

The act itself dates to 1856, in the year one thousand eight hundred and fifty-six as the text puts it. It makes Samuel Gregg, William Wesselhoeft, Luther Clark, George Russell, Milton Fuller, John A. Tarbell, and David Thayer, with their peers, a body under the society's name. Powers and duties follow the forty-fourth chapter of the Revised Statutes. Readers get a plain record of how a school of homeopathic doctors gained legal form in Massachusetts.
the-inner-life-part-3-from-the-works-of-:
John Greenleaf Whittier's prose on the inner life fills this third part. The contents list nine essays. They treat the agency of evil and Hamlet among the graves. Swedenborg and the better land appear. Dora Greenwell and the Society of Friends follow. John Woolman's Journal gets an essay. Haverford College closes the list. The opening essay dates from 1843. It first appeared in the Democratic Review. Its subject is the origin of evil.

Whittier calls that problem the darkest one in life. Life hangs about with wonders and dark riddles, he writes. Easy answers blame human passion and chance. He refuses to rest there. Even gross materialism, he notes, fears unseen powers. It senses a spirit passing before its face. The Quaker poet works out his faith in prose here. Old beliefs in Satan and witchcraft face a thoughtful test.
the-letters-of-robert-browning-and-eliza:
Robert Browning and Elizabeth Barrett wrote to each other through 1845 and 1846, before their marriage and flight to Italy. Volume one appeared in London in 1900, in a fourth impression with portraits and facsimiles. Their son supplies a note explaining why the letters reached print at all.

He says the choice lay between publishing them or destroying them, since his father kept every letter in an inlaid box after his mother death. The courtship here unfolds in daily writing, as two poets move from formal praise toward trust, love, and secret plans.
the-stark-munro-letters-being-series-of-:
A. Conan Doyle edited and arranged these twelve letters. Dr. J. Stark Munro wrote them to Herbert Swanborough. Swanborough was a former fellow student. He lived in Lowell, Massachusetts. The letters date from 1881 to 1884. Swanborough's covering note praises the letters. He calls them a plain account of a young man's troubles. Those troubles come at the start of a career. He hopes another young man will gain strength from them.

The first letter, headed Home and dated March 30, 1881, tells Bertie how much Munro has missed the one man to whom he could open his whole mind. He then begins at the beginning with Cullingworth, a figure from their university days whom Swanborough, outside the athletic set, may never have known.
the-story-of-kennett:
Bayard Taylor addresses this novel's prologue to his friends and neighbours. They live in Kennett, Pennsylvania. Taylor was born in that country. He spent many happy years there. He warns them that truth and fiction are woven together in the story. They live in the very houses of the tale. They work the very fields he gives his actors. Many will recognize real people behind the characters. Sandy Flash and Deb Smith are two of them.

Taylor copied the pastoral landscapes field for field and tree for tree, used only dialect he had himself heard, and drew customs true to the time though now obsolete. The chief incidents of the last chapter have a source. A woman gave them to Taylor on her death-bed. He shaped her character into Martha Deane. About the rest he asks leave to keep his own counsel.
tutt-and-mr-tutt:
Arthur Train's Tutt and Mr. Tutt, dated 1919, collects stories of the law firm Tutt and Tutt. The contents list The Human Element, Mock Hen and Mock Turtle, Samuel and Delilah, and The Dog Andrew. Wile versus guile and a piece called Lallapalooza Limited round out the seven tales.

The first story opens in the partners' office, where the junior Tutt despairs of a new client. Serafino, held in the Tombs, freely says he killed a man and would kill him again. Grand larceny and forgery the young lawyer can bear, but a cheerful murder client drives him to distraction. Train, himself a prosecutor, writes legal comedy from inside the courtroom world.
